title: Iran and the US Agreed to Stand Down. India's 9 Million Gulf Workers — and Its Oil Lifeline — Are Watching.
excerpt: A weekend of missiles and air-raid sirens in Kuwait and Bahrain gives way to a fragile promise to resume talks in Qatar on Tuesday
body:
The tit-for-tat strikes that rattled the Persian Gulf over the past four days appear to be over — at least for now.

On Sunday, Iran and the United States agreed to halt recent hostilities and resume negotiations over the Strait of Hormuz, raising hopes that the fragile 14-point peace accord signed on June 17 might yet survive. Talks are set to continue Tuesday in Qatar, where both sides will negotiate "all areas" of the memorandum of understanding that was meant to reopen the world's most critical oil shipping chokepoint.

"Both sides will stand down for now and vessels can move freely," a U.S. official said.

The diplomatic reset follows a dangerous weekend of escalation. After an Iranian projectile struck a cargo vessel in Hormuz on Thursday, both Washington and Tehran accused the other of breaking the interim ceasefire. The U.S. struck Iranian targets; Iran responded early Sunday with missiles and drones aimed at American military sites in Kuwait and Bahrain. Kuwait intercepted two ballistic missiles. Bahrain said an Iranian attack damaged a residential building in Muharraq province, though no casualties were reported.

## What This Means for India



> **"Talks are set to continue Tuesday in Qatar, where both sides will negotiate "all areas" of the memorandum of understanding that was meant to reopen the world's most critical oil shipping chokepoint."**


For New Delhi, the de-escalation is a reprieve — but a precarious one. India imports roughly 85 percent of its crude oil, and before the war, nearly 17 percent of the world's seaborne oil passed through Hormuz daily. With the strait largely choked off since February, India has already burned through strategic reserves and the rupee plunged to a record 96.96 against the dollar in April, forcing the Reserve Bank of India to sell nearly $9 billion in foreign exchange to shore up the currency.


![Persian Gulf — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/be/PersianGulf_vue_satellite_du_golfe_persique.jpg/3840px-PersianGulf_vue_satellite_du_golfe_persique.jpg)


The government recently directed ONGC to build a $1.6 billion strategic petroleum reserve expansion in Mangaluru, and Modi himself has publicly urged citizens to cut gold purchases, postpone foreign holidays, and carpool — an austerity appeal he said on Sunday's Mann Ki Baat has been widely embraced.

## 9 Million Indians in the Crossfire

But India's largest exposure in the Gulf is human, not just economic. Roughly 9 million Indian nationals live and work across the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Oman, and Qatar — the single largest diaspora concentration anywhere in the world. When Iranian missiles hit Kuwait and Bahrain early Sunday, millions of those workers woke to air-raid sirens for the second time in weeks.

India's Ministry of External Affairs has maintained "Operation Kaveri 2.0" standby contingency plans for mass evacuation since the war began in February, and the parliamentary standing committee on external affairs has separately been briefed on repatriation readiness. But the sheer scale — think every resident of New York City, plus a few million more — makes a full evacuation logistically staggering.

## Oil Markets Will Be Watching Qatar

If the Qatar talks produce a durable arrangement for vessel passage, Brent crude — which briefly dipped below its February 27 level last week on earlier peace signals — could retreat further, relieving inflationary pressure on the Indian economy. But the track record is not encouraging: the June 17 accord lasted barely twelve days before both sides claimed violations.

The RBI's extraordinary $55 billion FCNR deposit scheme, designed to pull diaspora dollar savings into Indian banks, now carries an additional dimension. If the Hormuz situation stabilises, the inflows could help rebuild depleted reserves. If it collapses again, those same reserves will face fresh pressure.

For the 9 million Indians in the Gulf and the 1.4 billion at home whose fuel bills, food prices, and financial stability hinge on this strait, the question is simple: will this ceasefire hold longer than the last one?
